entities.name: Marcus Valerius Messala Corvinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus (64 BCE – 8 CE) was a pivotal Roman statesman, general, orator, and patron of arts during the tumultuous transition from the Roman Republic to the Augustan Principate. A scion of the distinguished Valerii Messallae, he initially sided with the republican cause against Octavian, fighting alongside Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BCE. His eventual reconciliation with Octavian, driven by pragmatism and a recognition of the new political realities, allowed him to become a trusted advisor and a significant cultural figure in the nascent Roman Empire, embodying the intellectual and artistic bridge between the old order and the new.

Following his initial opposition, Messalla Corvinus served with distinction under Octavian, participating in key military campaigns that solidified Octavian's power. He held the consulship in 31 BCE, the same year as the decisive Battle of Actium, though he was not present at the battle itself. His military prowess was evident in his command in Aquitaine (28-27 BCE), where he quelled a rebellion and earned a triumph, demonstrating his continued value to the Augustan regime. Beyond his military and political contributions, Messalla was renowned for his forensic oratory, often compared to Cicero, and for his administrative acumen, notably serving as curator aquarum (superintendent of the aqueducts) in 11 BCE, a role later held by Sextus Julius Frontinus.
